source.title: The intriguing role of module criticality in the generalization of deep networks
source.authors: Niladri S. Chatterji; Behnam Neyshabur; Hanie Sedghi

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures whether a module criticality score tracks the training–test generalization gap across architectures and widths, using its own rewind and perturbation measurements. This is a related measurement rather than a direct test of most mapped interventions.
record.gate_note: The study measures training and test error, compares architecture-level generalization gaps with complexity measures, and tests whether module criticality ranks those gaps. Rows are limited to those results. Rewinding patterns and activation similarity are reported, but do not directly measure a claim version’s named outcome.
record.test_reason: Tables 2–3 bear on V3: convolutional architectures have smaller generalization gaps than fully connected networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The paper treats training error as very low, making these gaps evidence about held-out performance. Its proposed module criticality measure does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate as a synthesis of Section 4 and Appendix D: module criticality predicts some architecture rankings better than the compared measures, but performs poorly across width-only ResNet18 variants. The conclusion also proposes architecture design and search as potential applications.
record.recipe_differences: This study evaluates a proposed complexity measure by rewinding modules toward initialization and adding Gaussian perturbations, then compares its ranking with empirical generalization error; it does not directly test the original mapped interventions in most versions. CIFAR experiments use SGD with momentum and weight decay, except the corrupted-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture family change the ranking result: network criticality performs better across varied architectures but poorly on the ResNet18 width sweep. Criticality is computed at varying error thresholds.

fits_no_version.finding: Network criticality ranks architecture-level gaps with Kendall's tau 0.55 on both datasets, outperforming the listed comparison measures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A measure combining distance along initialization-to-trained-weight paths with module-wise noise tolerance can predict some architecture-level generalization rankings.

fits_no_version.finding: Network criticality ranks ResNet18 width variants inversely to their generalization gaps: tau −1 on CIFAR-10 and −0.66 on CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Module-based network criticality fails to predict generalization rankings across these channel-width variants.

record.problems: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the empirical comparisons. The architecture-ranking experiments use single reported values; the authors state that the measure performs poorly on width-only differences. The claim that test error does not improve under convex combination plus Gaussian perturbation is stated as a conjecture.
record.rows_left_out: No row was created for individual module rewinding plots or activation-pattern similarity: those results concern train-error changes or representation similarity and do not directly measure the claim versions’ named generalization outcomes. The paper’s cited prior results were excluded.

untested.parts: Almost-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance held-out performance on random labels. The 20% label-corruption comparison does not establish this combination.
Held-out error beyond an established zero-training-error width threshold; the reported ResNet width sweeps do not identify that threshold and use weight decay.
Attribution of the advantage to local connectivity, learned sparse connections, and initialization from trained convolutional networks.
Held-out performance comparisons between adaptive optimizers and SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and their effects on held-out error.

Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures. Module criticality combines rewinding distance and isotropic perturbations instead.
Removing highly memorized examples versus randomly selected examples and retraining.

missing.what: Architecture-specific gap values needed for the convolutional-versus-FCN comparison are omitted from the row values. Expand R1 and R2 into architecture-specific results. Separate training and test errors are not supplied in these tables.
missing.locator: Tables 2–3; Section 3's low-training-error premise; Appendix C

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V3. Its gap comparisons support the architectural performance finding without isolating its mechanism. Remove both V7 verdicts: failure of this distinct criticality measure does not challenge magnitude-aware sharpness.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization versus natural-label generalization under the same recipes.
A width sweep past the interpolation threshold in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained without explicit regularization.
A controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison isolating local connectivity and the specified initialization comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers’ held-out performance relative to SGD under the optimizer tuning conditions in the version.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets and the effects of recipe adaptations.
The effect of adding or removing dropout, alone or with weight decay, on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness compared with norm- and margin-based measures under the specific CIFAR-10 and SVHN, no-augmentation conditions in the version.
Removing memorized examples and comparing retraining outcomes with random-example removal.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared network criticality with generalization error across architectures on CIFAR-10; criticality is based on module perturbation along the initialization-to-trained-weight path.

conditions.value: ResNet18, ResNet34, ResNet50, ResNet101, DenseNet121, VGG11, VGG16, FCN (I), FCN (II)

rows.measure: Generalization error (test error minus training error); Kendall’s τ between network criticality ranking and generalization error ranking
rows.value: ResNet18 GE 4.61%; Net. Criticality 2.2e5. Overall Kendall’s τ = 0.55.
rows.note: Across the nine architectures, the criticality ranking agrees better with generalization error ranking than the other listed measures, but it fails to rank ResNet34, ResNet50, DenseNet121, VGG11, and FCN (II) correctly. The table gives per-architecture values and one aggregate τ.
rows.check: The row mixes a ResNet18 result with an aggregate criticality correlation. For V3, record the architecture comparison: convolutional GE ranges from 4.61% to 8.51%, versus 29.83% and 26.45% for FCNs. These are generalization gaps, not separately reported test errors. Network criticality is a different measure from V7.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 architectures trained from scratch using momentum SGD, augmentation and weight decay
relationships.reason: R1: all seven convolutional architectures have smaller gaps (4.61–8.51%) than either FCN (26.45–29.83%); interpreting this as held-out superiority relies on the text's low-training-error premise.
relationships.display_finding: The gaps between training and test performance were 4.61–8.51% for convolutional networks, versus 26.45–29.83% for FCNs. Inferring better test performance from these gaps requires low training error.
